result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.add_random_geometric_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add a random geometric graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L2736-L2848){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.add_random_geometric_graph( n, radius, dim=2, p_norm=2.0, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Random geometric graph](/assets/graphs/struct-geometric.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A random geometric graph: ten nodes placed as points in the plane, with edges only between pairs closer than a fixed connection threshold. One central node is drawn in the accent color and encircled by a faint dashed radius that shows the connection distance; every edge from that node lies inside the circle." width="100%"} Places `n` nodes uniformly at random in the unit hypercube and connects nodes whose distance is at most the value provided in `radius=`. This creates spatial networks where nearby points are more likely to be connected. Random geometric graphs are useful for modeling: - wireless networks (nodes in radio range) - social networks (geographically close individuals) - biological networks (spatially proximate cells) - ad-hoc networks and sensor networks ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes to add. [radius]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Maximum distance for edge creation. Nodes within this distance are connected. Must be non-negative. [dim]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of dimensions for the unit hypercube (default `2`). Use `2` for planar graphs, `3` for spatial networks. [p_norm]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Minkowski distance parameter (default `2.0` for Euclidean). Common values are `1.0` (Manhattan), `2.0` (Euclidean), `inf` (Chebyshev). [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for reproducibility. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `radius=` is negative, `dim=` < `1`, or `p_norm=` <= `0`. ::: ## Properties {.doc-properties} - **Undirected**: all edges are bidirectional. - **Spatial embedding**: nodes have positions in `[0, 1]^dim`. - **Node labels**: position stored as JSON array, e.g., `"[0.234, 0.567]"`. - **Local clustering**: high clustering due to geometric proximity. - **Threshold behavior**: graph connectivity exhibits phase transition as radius increases past a critical threshold. ## Complexity {.doc-complexity} - Time: `O(n²)` for distance comparisons (naive algorithm) - Space: `O(n × dim)` for positions plus O(edges) for graph ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes are scattered uniformly at random in the unit square, and only those within `radius=` of each other get connected: ::: {#58b6c413 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_random_geometric_graph( n=100, radius=0.2, seed=23 ) graph.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 100 ``` ::: ::: Each node's label records its coordinates, so the spatial layout stays inspectable after construction: ::: {#61187a17 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} node_id = graph.get_node_ids(limit=1)[0] graph.get_label_from_id(node_id) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` '[0.559436, 0.483903]' ``` ::: ::: Raising `dim=` embeds nodes in 3D space instead of 2D, which is useful for modeling physical or volumetric proximity: ::: {#e9c4a89b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} spatial_graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_random_geometric_graph( n=50, radius=0.3, dim=3, seed=123 ) spatial_graph.count_nodes(), spatial_graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (50, 88) ``` ::: ::: Switching to `p_norm=1.0` measures distance with the Manhattan (taxicab) metric instead of Euclidean distance, which changes which nodes count as "nearby" and therefore how many edges result: ::: {#4a5f81ea .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} manhattan_graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_random_geometric_graph( n=100, radius=0.25, p_norm=1.0, seed=23 ) manhattan_graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 531 ``` ::: :::
